newsitem.title: USA: Greenway play for Outboard welcomed, but puzzling.
newsitem.headline: Greenway play for Outboard welcomed, but puzzling.

text.p: Investors on Monday greeted Greenway Partners' statement that it may make an offer for Outboard Marine Corp as welcome, if puzzling, news.

Greenway, a New York-based investment group, said in a filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission that it was considering an offer for Outboard that could top a pending, $16-per-share offer from Detroit Diesel Corp.

"This is just an absolute joke for that franchise to be valued at $16 ... If you can find somebody who can run this company, it's worth a lot more," said James Schmitt, an analyst and investor at Westcountry Financial in California.
Shares in Waukegan, Ill.-based Outboard -- the largest U.S. maker of outboard engines and second-largest boat maker -- were up 1/8 to 16-1/8 on moderate volume late Monday.

Outboard declined to comment. A spokeswoman for Detroit Diesel, based in Detroit, said, "We have a tender offer that's outstanding and (Detroit Diesel) shares are pending registration. We, therefore, have no comment."
Detroit Diesel shares were down 2/16 at 25-5/16.
Greenway, which owns about two million shares of Outboard, or about 9.9 percent of the total outstanding stock, could not immediately be reached for further comment.

Analysts said Greenway acquired its stake in Outboard earlier this year in the high teens to low 20s, as did speculators who had wagered that it would be acquired for much more than the price offered last month by Detroit Diesel.
That $16-per-share cash-and-stock bid was seen as a "take-under" because it came in below the market price and well below the hopes of those looking for a quick killing.
"For a change, the speculators got hurt," said Cowen & Co industry analyst Harold Vogel. "The company might be worth more (than $16), but it can't be worth that much more."

Detroit Diesel's interest in Outboard was not seen as obvious when its bid was made. Controlled by the Penske group, Detroit Diesel makes truck engines and other equipment, but has little or no experience in recreational boats.
Greenway's attraction to Outboard was viewed as even more difficult to fathom, however, analysts said.
"I don't know what a financial buyer sees in this," Vogel said. "What is (Greenway) going to do with Outboard? These are financial guys, not guys who are going to run the company."
He said, "You could make better use of the assets (of Outboard) if you attach them to an operating company, like Detroit Diesel. It's a better fit in a lot of ways."

If Greenway can find an operating team with Penske's know-how, but deeper pockets, Schmitt said buying Outboard could make sense. "Financial buyers have a way of getting the right guy to run the company," he said.
